analysis.one_liner: Ends the ability of US corporations to avoid US tax on profits booked overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 9, 2017 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: US companies can park profits in overseas subsidiaries and defer paying US tax on them, sometimes indefinitely. This bill would tax foreign profits of US companies as they are earned, collect a one-time tax on profits already stockpiled offshore, and tighten several other rules used to shift income out of the US — including special breaks that large oil companies use when paying foreign governments, interest-deduction tactics, and 'inversions' where a US company merges with a foreign one to change its tax address. It never received a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers. Closing these avenues would raise federal revenue from profitable corporations, easing pressure to fund the government through taxes on individuals. Domestic-only companies, which cannot shift profits abroad, would also compete on more even terms.

how_it_helps.text: Taxes the foreign income of US companies as it is earned instead of allowing it to be deferred indefinitely while parked in overseas subsidiaries [S2][S3].
Requires a one-time tax on the accumulated offshore earnings companies had already deferred, payable in up to eight installments [S3].
Denies the foreign tax credit to large oil companies that pay levies to foreign governments while receiving a specific economic benefit from them, closing a dual-capacity loophole [S2][S3].

Treats foreign corporations whose management and control sit in the United States as domestic corporations for tax purposes, and tightens rules on inversions so that deals after May 2014 in which former US owners hold more than 50 percent of the new entity are taxed as domestic [S2][S3].
Limits interest deductions for members of multinational groups with excess domestic indebtedness, curbing a common technique for loading US companies with debt to erase taxable income [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: US multinationals with large offshore profit centers, large integrated oil companies, and foreign-domiciled companies that are effectively run from the United States. Wealthy shareholders of those companies bear the tax through lower after-tax returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: US multinationals and large oil companies

drawbacks.text: Immediate taxation of foreign income could make US-headquartered multinationals less competitive against foreign rivals that do not face the same rule, a cost that could fall partly on US workers and shareholders [S3].
The one-time inclusion of previously deferred earnings is a large retroactive levy on profits earned under the old rules, payable over at most eight years [S3].
Reinstating the per-country foreign tax credit can raise tax bills for companies operating in high-tax countries, adding compliance complexity that small firms feel more than large ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would raise substantial revenue from profitable corporations and close well-documented avoidance routes, with the main downside being the competitiveness concern for US multinationals and the retroactive nature of the offshore-earnings tax. The design is aggressive but coherent; the bigger obstacle was political, since it drew a single cosponsor and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never considered it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on March 9, 2017, with Sen. Schatz as the only cosponsor [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on March 9, 2017 [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, or vote — and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and large oil companies kept the ability to defer US tax on foreign profits and use the other avoidance channels the bill targeted. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's death, since the revenue it would have raised was never collected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals and oil companies kept the loopholes

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on March 9, 2017.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; he was its only cosponsor.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was one Independent and one Democrat; no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would end deferral of US tax on foreign profits and tax previously deferred offshore earnings, directly costing multinationals that shift profits abroad. Their gain in the status quo is revenue ordinary taxpayers otherwise have to make up.
The bill denies the foreign tax credit to big oil companies that pay foreign levies tied to receiving economic benefits, closing a break specific to their industry.

industries.industry: Foreign-domiciled companies managed from the US (including investment funds)
industries.note: The bill would tax foreign corporations whose management and control are primarily in the United States as if they were domestic, ending a structuring advantage for offshore headquarters.
The bill would eliminate some cross-border structuring work but add new compliance regimes (installment elections, interest-expense allocations) that generate planning and filing work.
